questiontext.text: A test path set satisfies Node Coverage but not Edge Coverage. What must be true?

answer.text: Every node is visited, but some edge is never traversed

feedback.text: Correct — edge coverage subsumes node coverage, not vice versa.
Then node coverage would already fail.
Prime path coverage would imply edge coverage.
With no branches, node coverage implies edge coverage.

generalfeedback.text: Edge coverage requires every edge; a branch can be skipped even when both its endpoints are visited via other paths.

questiontext.text: In graph-based testing, a test path is a path that:

answer.text: Starts at an initial node and ends at a final node of the graph

feedback.text: Correct — a test path represents one complete execution from entry to exit.

answer.text: Visits every node of the graph exactly once

feedback.text: That is a Hamiltonian path, not a test path.

answer.text: Is any single edge of the graph

feedback.text: A single edge is a path of length 1, but a test path must run from an initial to a final node.
A test path may repeat nodes (e.g. loop iterations); only simple paths forbid repeats.

generalfeedback.text: A test path is a path from an initial node to a final node; running a test case executes exactly one test path.

questiontext.text: Classic statement coverage corresponds to which graph-coverage criterion on the control-flow graph?

feedback.text: Correct — executing every statement means visiting every node.
Edge coverage corresponds to branch coverage, which is stronger.
Prime path coverage is much stronger than statement coverage.
Complete path coverage is generally infeasible and far stronger.

generalfeedback.text: Nodes model basic blocks/statements, so statement coverage is exactly node coverage.

questiontext.text: Classic branch coverage corresponds to which graph-coverage criterion?

feedback.text: Correct — every branch outcome is an edge that must be traversed.
Node coverage corresponds to statement coverage, which is weaker.
Edge-pair coverage requires paths of length up to 2, which is stronger than branch coverage.
All-uses is a data-flow criterion, not the same as branch coverage.

generalfeedback.text: Each decision outcome is an outgoing edge, so branch coverage is exactly edge coverage.

questiontext.text: On any graph, a test set that satisfies Edge Coverage also satisfies Node Coverage.

feedback.text: Correct — traversing every edge visits every node that has an incident edge.
Edge coverage subsumes node coverage: covering all edges necessarily visits all reachable nodes.

generalfeedback.text: Edge Coverage subsumes Node Coverage; the converse does not hold.

questiontext.text: Complete Path Coverage is infeasible on any control-flow graph that contains a loop.

feedback.text: Correct — a loop yields infinitely many paths.
Loops create unbounded path counts, so complete path coverage cannot be finitely satisfied.

generalfeedback.text: A loop lets a path revisit the same node arbitrarily many times, so the set of complete test paths is unbounded — Complete Path Coverage can never be finitely satisfied whenever the graph has a loop.

questiontext.text: A simple path is a path in which:

answer.text: No node appears more than once, except that the first and last nodes may be the same

feedback.text: Correct — this allows a loop to close but forbids all other repeats.

answer.text: No node ever repeats under any circumstances

feedback.text: Simple paths may begin and end at the same node (a round trip).

answer.text: Every node of the graph is visited

feedback.text: That describes a spanning path, not a simple path.

answer.text: Every edge is used at most once

feedback.text: That is a trail; simple paths constrain node repeats, not edge repeats.

generalfeedback.text: A simple path has no repeated nodes, with the single exception that the first and last node may coincide.

questiontext.text: Satisfying Node Coverage guarantees that every branch (decision outcome) has been exercised.

feedback.text: Correct — node coverage can be met while an edge (branch outcome) is never taken.
Node coverage only requires visiting nodes; an untaken branch can still leave every node visited via other paths.

generalfeedback.text: Node coverage does not imply edge coverage, so some branch outcomes may go untested.

questiontext.text: A control-flow graph on nodes 1..4 has directed edges 1→2, 2→3, 3→4, 2→4. How many directed edges does it have?

feedback.text: Correct — the edge list contains exactly four edges.
Recount — there are four edges listed.
Recount — there are only four edges listed.
Recount — there are only four edges listed.

generalfeedback.text: Edge Coverage needs one test requirement per edge; here that is 4 edges.

questiontext.text: A control-flow graph on nodes 1..5 has directed edges 1→2, 2→3, 3→4, 4→5, 2→5. How many directed edges does it have?

feedback.text: Correct — five edges are listed.
Recount — there are five edges listed.
Recount — there are only five edges listed.
Recount — there are only five edges listed.

generalfeedback.text: Count each directed edge once; the list is the complete edge set.

questiontext.text: A control-flow graph has nodes 1..5 and edges 1→2, 2→3, 2→4, 3→5, 4→5. How many test requirements does Node Coverage impose?

feedback.text: Correct — one requirement per node, and there are 5 nodes.
Node coverage counts nodes (5), not edges.
That counts branch points, not all nodes.
Node coverage has one requirement per node, so 5, not the number of node pairs.

generalfeedback.text: Node Coverage requires visiting each node, so the number of requirements equals the number of nodes.

questiontext.text: A graph has edges 1→2, 2→3, 2→4. How many length-2 paths u→v→w (pairs of edges sharing a middle node v) exist?

feedback.text: Correct — 1→2→3 and 1→2→4.
There are two: 1→2→3 and 1→2→4.
Only edges sharing a middle node count; there are two such pairs.
Node 2 is the middle of two length-2 paths.

generalfeedback.text: For each edge u→v, count each edge v→w; here node 2 feeds two outgoing edges, giving 2 length-2 paths.

questiontext.text: A graph has edges 1→2, 2→3, 3→4, 2→4. How many length-2 paths u→v→w exist?

feedback.text: There are three: 1→2→3, 1→2→4, 2→3→4.
Recount — only three edge pairs share a middle node.
Nodes 2 and 3 each serve as a middle node, giving three pairs total.

generalfeedback.text: Middle node 2 gives 1→2→3 and 1→2→4; middle node 3 gives 2→3→4; total 3.

questiontext.text: A control-flow graph has edges 1→2, 1→3, 2→4, 3→4. How many test requirements does Edge Coverage impose?

feedback.text: Correct — one requirement per edge, and there are 4 edges.
Edge coverage counts edges (4), not nodes.
That counts the number of complete paths, not edges.
There are only 4 edges to cover.

generalfeedback.text: Edge Coverage requires traversing each edge, so the number of requirements equals the number of edges.

questiontext.text: Which of the following structural criteria is the weakest (least demanding)?

feedback.text: Correct — node coverage is subsumed by all the others.
Edge coverage subsumes node coverage, so it is stronger.
Edge-pair coverage subsumes edge and node coverage.
Prime path coverage is one of the strongest structural criteria.

generalfeedback.text: The structural chain is Prime Path → Edge-Pair → Edge → Node, so Node Coverage is the weakest.

questiontext.text: A prime path is a simple path that:

answer.text: Is not a proper subpath of any other simple path

feedback.text: Correct — maximal simple paths.

answer.text: Starts at the entry node and ends at the exit node

feedback.text: That describes a complete test path, not a prime path.
That is a Hamiltonian path.
A prime path may begin and end at the same node (a loop boundary).

generalfeedback.text: Prime paths are simple paths (no repeated nodes except possibly first = last) that are maximal — not proper subpaths of any other simple path.

questiontext.text: Which criterion subsumes Edge Coverage on a graph with at least one edge?

feedback.text: Correct — covering every path of length ≤ 2 covers every length-1 path.
Node coverage is weaker than edge coverage.
Statement coverage corresponds to node coverage.
Edge-pair, prime path and complete path all do.

generalfeedback.text: Edge-pair coverage requires all length-≤2 paths, which includes every single edge.

questiontext.text: In data-flow coverage, a DU pair for variable x is:

answer.text: A definition of x and a use of x reachable by a def-clear path

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: Any two statements that mention x

feedback.text: Mentions alone don't form a DU pair.
The second assignment kills the first definition.

answer.text: A use of x followed by its definition

feedback.text: Order is definition first, then use.

generalfeedback.text: A DU pair (d, u) needs a path from d to u with no intervening redefinition of x — a def-clear path.

questiontext.text: stvisual reduces the selected test-path set with a greedy approximation of which classic problem? (two words)

feedback.text: Correct — greedy set cover.
Correct.

generalfeedback.text: Choosing a minimal set of test paths covering all requirements is the (NP-hard) set-cover problem; the tool uses the greedy approximation.

questiontext.text: A CFG has edges 1→2, 1→3, 2→4, 3→4 (node 1 initial, node 4 final). Which of the following is a prime path?

feedback.text: Correct — it is a maximal simple path (not a subpath of any longer simple path).
2→4 is a proper subpath of the simple path 1→2→4, so it is not prime.
1→2 is a proper subpath of 1→2→4, so it is not prime.
There is no edge 4→3, so this is not even a valid path.

generalfeedback.text: The prime paths of this graph are 1→2→4 and 1→3→4; shorter simple paths are subpaths of these.

questiontext.text: A round-trip path is:

answer.text: A prime path of nonzero length whose first and last nodes are the same

feedback.text: Correct — it captures one traversal of a loop.

answer.text: Any path from the initial node to a final node

feedback.text: That is a general test path, not specifically a round trip.

answer.text: A path that visits every node twice

feedback.text: Round trips are simple paths; nodes are not visited twice except the shared endpoint.

answer.text: Any pair of edges u→v and v→u

feedback.text: A round trip is a prime path returning to its start, not merely a back-and-forth edge pair.

generalfeedback.text: A round-trip path is a prime path with nonzero length that starts and ends at the same node; Simple/Complete Round Trip Coverage are built on these.

questiontext.text: A path from a definition of x to a use of x is def-clear (with respect to x) when:

answer.text: No node on the path between the def and the use redefines x

feedback.text: Correct — the original definition still reaches the use.
Branches are irrelevant; what matters is no intervening redefinition of x.

answer.text: x is used at every node on the path

feedback.text: Def-clear concerns redefinitions, not uses along the way.

answer.text: The path is a prime path

feedback.text: Def-clear is about redefinitions, unrelated to whether the path is prime.

generalfeedback.text: A def-clear path w.r.t. x has no redefinition of x strictly between the def and the use, so the def reaches the use.

questiontext.text: Which criterion does Prime Path Coverage subsume?

feedback.text: Correct — prime paths of length ≥ 2 cover all length-≤2 subpaths.
Structural prime-path coverage does not subsume data-flow criteria.
Complete path coverage is stronger and subsumes prime path coverage, not the reverse.
All-uses is a data-flow criterion; prime-path coverage does not subsume it.

generalfeedback.text: Prime Path Coverage subsumes Edge-Pair, Edge, and Node coverage, but not the data-flow criteria.

questiontext.text: Which statement about the data-flow criteria All-Defs and All-Uses is correct?

feedback.text: Correct — reaching every use of every def implies reaching at least one use of every def.
The subsumption runs the other way: All-Uses is stronger.
All-Uses is strictly stronger when a def reaches more than one use.
All-Uses does subsume All-Defs.

generalfeedback.text: All-Defs requires each def to reach at least one use; All-Uses requires each def to reach every one of its uses — so All-Uses subsumes All-Defs.

questiontext.text: Edge-Pair Coverage requires touring every reachable path of length up to 2 (i.e. every single edge and every pair of adjacent edges).

feedback.text: Correct — edge-pair coverage is defined over paths of length ≤ 2.
Edge-pair coverage is exactly the set of reachable paths of length up to 2.

generalfeedback.text: Edge-Pair Coverage tours all reachable length-≤2 paths, which is why it subsumes Edge Coverage (length-1 paths).

questiontext.text: A CFG on nodes 1..5 has edges 1→2, 1→3, 2→3, 2→4, 3→4, 4→5. How many length-2 paths u→v→w exist?

feedback.text: Recount — there are six length-2 paths.
Recount — only six edge pairs share a middle node.
Middle nodes 2, 3, and 4 together yield six length-2 paths.

generalfeedback.text: Per middle node, multiply in-degree by out-degree: node 2 = 1×2 = 2, node 3 = 2×1 = 2, node 4 = 2×1 = 2; total 6.

questiontext.text: A CFG on nodes 1..5 has edges 1→2, 1→3, 1→5, 2→3, 2→4, 4→5. How many length-2 paths u→v→w exist?

feedback.text: Recount — only three edge pairs share a middle node.
Node 2 alone yields two, and node 4 yields a third.
That counts edges, not length-2 paths.

generalfeedback.text: Only middle nodes with both an incoming and an outgoing edge count: node 2 gives 1→2→3 and 1→2→4, node 4 gives 2→4→5.

questiontext.text: In graph-based testing, a test requirement is:

answer.text: A specific structural element (e.g. a node, edge, or prime path) that a test path must tour

feedback.text: Correct — a criterion defines a set of test requirements.

answer.text: A single test case with its input values

feedback.text: That is a test case; a requirement is what the case must satisfy.

answer.text: The expected output of the program

feedback.text: That is an oracle, not a coverage requirement.

answer.text: A complete path from entry to exit

feedback.text: A complete path may satisfy several requirements, but a requirement is the element to be toured.

generalfeedback.text: A coverage criterion is a rule that yields a set of test requirements; each requirement is a structure that some test path must tour.

questiontext.text: When a required prime path cannot be toured directly by any complete test path, a common practice is to:

answer.text: Tour it with a sidetrip/detour if possible (best-effort touring)

feedback.text: Correct — best-effort touring allows sidetrips to reach otherwise hard requirements.

answer.text: Delete the prime path from the graph

feedback.text: Requirements are not removed from the graph; touring is relaxed instead.
A single hard requirement does not make the criterion unusable; best-effort touring is used.

answer.text: Add a new edge so the path becomes direct

feedback.text: The graph models the program and is not altered to satisfy a requirement.

generalfeedback.text: Best-effort touring permits sidetrips (detours) so requirements that cannot be toured directly can still be covered where feasible.

questiontext.text: All-Defs Coverage requires that, for each definition of a variable:

answer.text: At least one def-clear path from that definition to some use is toured

feedback.text: Correct — each def must reach at least one use.

answer.text: A def-clear path to every use is toured

feedback.text: That is All-Uses, which is stronger than All-Defs.

answer.text: Every simple path from the definition is toured

feedback.text: That resembles All-DU-Paths, not All-Defs.

answer.text: The definition is executed at least once

feedback.text: That is only node coverage of the def; All-Defs also requires reaching a use.

generalfeedback.text: All-Defs requires each def to reach at least one use via a def-clear path; All-Uses strengthens this to every use.

questiontext.text: On a graph with at least one edge, which criterion is subsumed by Prime Path Coverage?

feedback.text: Correct — prime paths of length ≥ 2 cover all length-≤2 subpaths.
Complete path coverage is generally infeasible and is not subsumed.
Data-flow criteria are not subsumed by structural prime-path coverage.
Prime path coverage does subsume edge and edge-pair coverage.

generalfeedback.text: Prime path coverage subsumes edge-pair and edge coverage; it does not subsume data-flow or complete-path criteria.

questiontext.text: Which chain correctly orders the data-flow criteria from strongest (subsumes) to weakest?

feedback.text: Correct — each subsumes the next.
This reverses the order; All-DU-Paths is the strongest.
All-DU-Paths subsumes All-Uses, so it must come first.
All-Defs is the weakest, so it cannot lead the chain.

generalfeedback.text: All-DU-Paths subsumes All-Uses, which subsumes All-Defs.

questiontext.text: Prime Path Coverage subsumes All-DU-Paths Coverage.

feedback.text: Correct — structural prime-path coverage does not subsume data-flow criteria.
Prime path coverage subsumes edge-pair/edge/node coverage, but not the data-flow criteria.

generalfeedback.text: Data-flow criteria depend on def-use relationships that structural prime-path coverage does not guarantee, so there is no subsumption.

questiontext.text: A test requirement is infeasible when:

answer.text: No test path that satisfies the program's semantics can tour it

feedback.text: Correct — infeasibility is about semantics, not graph structure.

answer.text: It requires more than one test case

feedback.text: Needing several cases does not make a requirement infeasible.

answer.text: It is a prime path longer than the number of nodes

feedback.text: Prime paths are simple, so their length is bounded; length alone is not infeasibility.
Loops make complete path coverage infinite, but do not by themselves make a requirement infeasible.

generalfeedback.text: An infeasible requirement cannot be toured by any semantically valid execution (e.g. contradictory branch conditions); coverage is measured against feasible requirements.

questiontext.text: A CFG has nodes 1..4 and edges 1→2, 1→3, 2→4, 3→4. How many prime paths does it have?

feedback.text: Correct — 1→2→4 and 1→3→4 are the only maximal simple paths.
The four edges are not all prime; each is a subpath of a longer simple path.
There are exactly two maximal simple paths.
That over-counts; shorter simple paths are subpaths of the two prime paths.

generalfeedback.text: Prime paths are maximal simple paths. Here they are 1→2→4 and 1→3→4; every shorter simple path is a subpath of one of these.

questiontext.text: A CFG on nodes 1..7 has edges 1→2, 1→3, 1→4, 2→3, 2→4, 2→5, 2→6, 3→4, 5→7. How many length-2 paths u→v→w exist?

feedback.text: Correct — enumerate edges out of each middle node.
Recount — there are seven length-2 paths.
That counts edges (9), not length-2 paths.
Recount — only seven edge pairs share a middle node.

generalfeedback.text: Per middle node, multiply in-degree by out-degree: node 2 = 1×4 = 4, node 3 = 2×1 = 2, node 5 = 1×1 = 1; total 4 + 2 + 1 = 7 length-2 paths.

questiontext.text: All-Uses subsumes All-Defs, but All-Defs does not subsume All-Uses.

feedback.text: Correct — the subsumption holds in one direction only.
All-Uses is strictly stronger: satisfying All-Defs need not reach every use.

generalfeedback.text: Reaching one use per def (All-Defs) does not imply reaching every use per def (All-Uses), so the subsumption is one-directional.

questiontext.text: How do Simple Round Trip Coverage and Complete Round Trip Coverage differ?

answer.text: Simple requires at least one round-trip path per reachable node that begins one; Complete requires all round-trip paths

feedback.text: Correct — Complete is the stronger of the two.

answer.text: Simple requires all round-trip paths; Complete requires just one

feedback.text: This reverses them — Complete requires all.
They differ: one asks for at least one, the other for all round trips.

answer.text: Simple ignores loops; Complete counts them once

feedback.text: Both are about round-trip (loop) paths; the difference is one vs all.

generalfeedback.text: Simple Round Trip Coverage needs one round-trip path for each node that starts one; Complete Round Trip Coverage needs every round-trip path, so it subsumes Simple.

questiontext.text: Among the structural criteria Node, Edge, Edge-Pair, Prime Path, and Complete Path Coverage, which subsumes all the others?

feedback.text: Correct — touring every path covers every node, edge, edge-pair and prime path (though it is usually infeasible).
Prime path coverage is subsumed by complete path coverage.
Edge-pair coverage is well below the top of the hierarchy.
Node coverage is the weakest of these criteria.

generalfeedback.text: Complete Path Coverage is the strongest structural criterion (Complete Path → Prime Path → Edge-Pair → Edge → Node), but is infeasible whenever loops are present.

questiontext.text: A single definition of x reaches two distinct uses u1 and u2 via def-clear paths. To satisfy All-Uses for this definition, a test set must:

answer.text: Tour a def-clear path to both u1 and u2

feedback.text: Correct — All-Uses requires reaching every reachable use of the definition.

answer.text: Tour a def-clear path to either u1 or u2

feedback.text: Reaching just one use satisfies All-Defs, not All-Uses.

answer.text: Tour every simple path to u1 and u2

feedback.text: That is All-DU-Paths, which is even stronger than All-Uses.
Executing the def alone does not reach its uses.

generalfeedback.text: All-Uses requires a def-clear path from the def to each of its reachable uses; here that means reaching both u1 and u2.

questiontext.text: When a path tours a subpath q with a sidetrip, it means:

answer.text: The path covers every edge of q in order, possibly leaving and rejoining q in between

feedback.text: Correct — a sidetrip covers all edges of q but may wander off and return.

answer.text: The path covers q with no extra edges at all

feedback.text: That is touring q directly, not with a sidetrip.

answer.text: The path skips some edges of q

feedback.text: A sidetrip still covers every edge of q; it only adds detours between them.

answer.text: The path reverses the direction of q

feedback.text: Sidetrips preserve q's edges and direction; they only insert extra excursions.

generalfeedback.text: Touring with a sidetrip covers all of q's edges in order while allowing detours away from and back onto q; direct touring uses no detours.

questiontext.text: A CFG has nodes 1..4 and edges 1→2, 2→3, 3→2, 2→4 (a while-loop shape). How many prime paths does it have?

feedback.text: Recount — the loop contributes the round trips 2→3→2 and 3→2→3 as well.
The two round-trip prime paths through the loop are easy to miss.
That over-counts; there are exactly five maximal simple paths.

generalfeedback.text: The prime paths are 1→2→3, 1→2→4, 3→2→4, and the two loop round trips 2→3→2 and 3→2→3 — five in total.

questiontext.text: On the path from a definition d of x to a use u of x, node m redefines x. What is the effect on the DU pair (d, u) along this path?

answer.text: This path is not def-clear for (d, u); d's value no longer reaches u here

feedback.text: Correct — the redefinition at m kills d before u.

answer.text: The DU pair (d, u) is still covered by this path

feedback.text: The redefinition means d's value does not reach u along this path.

answer.text: m becomes part of the same DU pair

feedback.text: m starts a new definition; it does not join (d, u).

answer.text: The use u is no longer a use of x

feedback.text: u is still a use of x; it is just reached by m's definition, not d's.

generalfeedback.text: A redefinition between d and u kills d, so the path is not def-clear w.r.t. x for (d, u); another def-clear path is needed to cover that pair.

questiontext.text: Which criterion is NOT subsumed by Edge-Pair Coverage?

feedback.text: Correct — prime path coverage is stronger, so edge-pair coverage does not subsume it.
Edge-pair coverage does subsume edge coverage.
Edge-pair coverage subsumes node coverage (via edge coverage).
Statement coverage equals node coverage, which edge-pair coverage subsumes.

generalfeedback.text: Subsumption goes Prime Path → Edge-Pair → Edge → Node; edge-pair coverage subsumes weaker criteria but not the stronger prime-path coverage.

questiontext.text: On a graph where every node has an incident edge, Prime Path Coverage subsumes Node Coverage.

feedback.text: Correct — by transitivity through edge-pair and edge coverage.
Prime Path → Edge-Pair → Edge → Node, so prime-path coverage subsumes node coverage.

generalfeedback.text: Subsumption is transitive: Prime Path subsumes Edge-Pair, which subsumes Edge, which subsumes Node.
